paras: The Barbour County whitecapping of 1903 was a campaign of threats and night violence by bands of white men, called "whitecaps," against Black farm laborers in Barbour County, Alabama, in the summer of 1903. Black laborers were reported driven off several plantations under threat of death, and federal officers arrested seven Barbour men in September. In January 1904 a federal grand jury indicted six of them for conspiring to intimidate four named Black residents.

The men later charged lived near the Zeiglers post office, in Beat 8 of the county, where the whitecapping was said to be "seriously demoralizing the labor of the county." A Montgomery dispatch said the cause was "said to be due to some overt acts of the negroes," but did not say who gave this explanation or what the acts were.

According to the federal prosecutor, between late July and mid-August 1903 the men went at night, without warrant or legal authority, to the house of Marion Shipman, "a reputable negro of family," who let them in to search for an alleged murderer. Several days later, before dawn, they returned and battered down his door; Shipman knocked one of them down but was seized, bound, gagged, beaten with a pistol and a gun, taken several miles down a road and lashed. The government did not describe its evidence concerning the other three named victims.

By August 21 a "well authenticated rumor" reached Montgomery of "a practical race war" in part of the county, with the labor on three or more large plantations run off by whitecaps. The gang was said to be "warning the blacks to leave under penalty of death."

About August 20 a prominent Barbour citizen asked Judge Thomas G. Jones of the federal court how to stop the whitecapping; Jones reportedly sent him to the governor, saying federal authorities should not do "what the state authorities ought to do." Federal officers acted nonetheless: by August 28 a United States deputy, J. F. Greene, was in the county with warrants, and the Montgomery Advertiser reported a federal investigation on September 2.

On September 15 seven Barbour men were brought before United States Commissioner Tutwiler at Troy and jailed pending hearings. One report said five were then held in $500 bond each; the Birmingham Age-Herald said seven were bound over.

On January 16, 1904, the federal grand jury indicted six men under Section 5508 of the Revised Statutes for conspiring to intimidate Albert Barefield, Marion Shipman, Hillard Turner and Nancy Miles, the first whitecapping cases there in a decade, according to the Advertiser. At the arraignment Judge Jones told five defendants that an earlier state trial for assault and battery on one victim gave them no plea of former jeopardy. One declared that he "jés naturally ain't guilty," and the men were released on bond pending a hearing; no report of a plea, trial or sentence was found.

All coverage found appeared in white papers, beginning with an August 22 Age-Herald note that a "race war" was "raging" and an Atlanta Constitution dispatch headed "White Caps Scare Negroes," whose subhead framed the matter as a labor problem. The Troy arrest wire ran in Georgia, Indiana and Kentucky papers under headlines such as "White Men Jailed as Whitecappers" and "Arrest of Night Riders for Terrorizing Blacks of Barbour County."

The Age-Herald remarked that the case showed "we have not yet outlived our reconstruction habits," while the Gainesville Star stressed that the accused were "prominent citizens." The Advertiser's January report, the only detailed account, ran under the subhead "Persecuted Negroes" and called the prosecutor's statements "remarkable," yet described the defendants as "rough and illiterate" with "not a bad face among the five men."

The September wire named seven accused, a later report five, and the January indictments six, adding Morgan Padgett and Richard Knowles and omitting Richard Mann, Wash Green and A. V. Norton. The indictment, as the later formal record, is the best evidence of who was finally charged.

reader.title: Barbour County whitecapping (1903)
bases: Every report calls the acts 'whitecapping' by 'whitecaps' or a 'gang' that drove Black laborers off Barbour farms by threats (A2, A4, A6), and the federal indictments charged conspiracy to intimidate named Black residents, including a night attack on one (A20).

Separate Montgomery specials (A2, A4), the Montgomery Advertiser (A5, A20) and the Troy arrest wire (A6, A11) agree that white men in Barbour County were driving Black residents away by threats and were prosecuted federally.

framing.detail: The Atlanta Constitution's 'White Caps Scare Negroes' and 'Labor ... Badly Demoralized' framed the episode as a labor problem and passed on an unattributed claim that Black residents' 'overt acts' caused it.
The Troy arrest wire ran under headlines such as 'White Men Jailed as Whitecappers' and 'Arrest of Night Riders for Terrorizing Blacks of Barbour County'.
The Birmingham Age-Herald said the binding over of the whitecappers 'reminds us that we have not yet outlived our reconstruction habits.'

The Montgomery Advertiser's subhead 'Persecuted Negroes' and its account of the prosecutor's 'remarkable statements' sat beside a sympathetic sketch of the defendants as 'rough and illiterate' men with 'not a bad face' among them.
